rv.q: James Macdonald’s magnificently modulated revival at the Theatre is a brilliant reminder of what an extraordinary feat Williams pulled off here.
Macdonald's superb revival, which boasts a majestic creeper-strewn mountain-top set by Rae Smith, rightly focuses on the central performances.
Good as they are, Williams outshines them both and is simply magnificent as the gentle Miss Jelkes.
He grows in the role impressively.
‘The Night of the Iguana’ is neither, though it’s a little of both.
James Macdonald's production is mostly becalmed.
But Owen’s central performance is two-dimensional.

But the flawed, fascinating evening belongs to Lia Williams and Breaking Bad star Anna Gunn. James MacDonald’s three-hour production balances thunderstorms with moments of quiet intensity, and leavens Williams’s tendency towards overkill with wry humour.
...this may not be vintage Williams, but it survives through its opportunities for actors and the author’s boundless charity.
Without a real charisma bomb fizzing away at the centre of the show, you’re free to observe how desperately slowly the first half builds.
As life's misfits find consolation and comfort in each other, I was truly moved.
And it's an emotionally generous production of a generous-spirited classic.
If human connection is this play's heart, then Williams as Hannah Jelkes is the pulse.
It’s quietly heartbreaking, a study in the melancholy of life’s misfits, and director James MacDonald’s sensitive West End staging, starring Clive Owen and Anna Gunn, is full of feeling.
I confess that although I admired every aspect of his handsome and brilliantly executed production, I couldn't get excited about it.

SET during one night at a rain-swept hotel in Mexico, The Night of the Iguana is a meandering exploration of human interaction and the hope, support and compassion that practical strangers can offer each other.

cn.t: Critics find this Tennessee Williams revival sensitively directed and well-acted, particularly praising Lia Williams, though opinions split on Clive Owen's brooding performance and the production's occasionally becalmed pacing.
